original_question: Find a perfect square such that subtracting from it 10 times its square root and then 10 dirhams still leaves a perfect square.
target_in_paper: §5.2, Problem 16: "Find a square number such that, if ten times its square root and ten dirhams are subtracted from it, the result is still a perfect square." ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))
correct_elements: Your draft is extremely close to the paper’s actual Problem 16: it keeps the same unknown object (a square number), the same operation (subtract ten times its square root and ten dirhams), and the same target condition (the remainder is again a perfect square). It is therefore already a near-paraphrase of the official statement in §5.2. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))
missing_details: The draft does not explicitly say whether the search is over positive integers, positive rationals, or another domain. The paper as a whole frames these problems in the setting of searching for integer or rational solutions, so the ambient domain should be made explicit in a stand-alone version. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))

The draft leaves the unknown unnamed. A stand-alone formulation should introduce variables, e.g. a square number N and another square number M, or equivalently x and y with N=x^2 and M=y^2. This is the natural algebraic unpacking of Problem 16 and matches the paper’s adjacent “Modern formulation” line. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))

The algebraic condition should be written explicitly: N - 10√N - 10 = M, with N and M perfect squares; equivalently x^2 - 10x - 10 = y^2 after writing N=x^2. This is an inference from the paper’s wording and its immediately following “Modern formulation” marker. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))

The draft does not make the existence quantifier explicit. A sharp research question should say whether one seeks at least one example, all solutions, or a proof of impossibility. The original problem statement is existential (“Find…”), so the stand-alone version should preserve that scope. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))

The phrase “10 dirhams” functions mathematically as the constant 10; in a modern stand-alone statement it helps to note that this is just the additive constant in the equation. This is implicit in the paper’s historical wording. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))
refined_question: Determine whether there exists a positive integer N that is a perfect square such that N - 10√N - 10 is also a perfect square; if so, exhibit such an N. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, writing N=x^2 and the remaining square as y^2, solve x^2 - 10x - 10 = y^2 in positive integers x,y. This is the standard algebraic unpacking of §5.2, Problem 16 and corresponds in substance to the paper’s adjacent “Modern formulation” line. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))
justification: This draft clearly targets Problem 16 in the paper’s list of thirty-three open problems, not a conjecture/proposition/theorem elsewhere in the article. The wording is almost verbatim: the paper’s §5.2 asks for a square number from which ten times its square root and ten dirhams are subtracted, leaving another perfect square. The main things needed to make your draft fully stand-alone are explicit variables, an explicit domain, and the precise equation encoded by the historical phrasing. The paper also places this item inside the organized list of Ibn al-Khawwām’s problems in §5, while the introduction states that the article studies such problems in the search for integer or rational solutions. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08400v1))
